subject: geography
title: Transport and Deposition
welcome_lead: Rivers don't just erode — they also carry and drop material. Learn the four ways rivers transport sediment and where it ends up.
meta_desc: KS3 Geography adventure on river transport (traction, suspension) and deposition.
final_note: Great work! You can now explain how rivers move and deposit material.

concepts.def: How rivers move eroded material downstream.
Large rocks rolling along the riverbed.
Small stones bouncing along the bed.
Fine particles carried within the water.
Dissolved minerals carried in the water.
When the river drops material it cannot carry.

walkthroughs.body_html:
• Traction: rolling big rocks.
  • Saltation: bouncing pebbles.
  • Suspension: fine silt floating.
  • Solution: dissolved minerals.
When a river loses energy — like during low flow or near the mouth — it can't carry its load. The heaviest material is dropped first.
Deposition creates floodplains, levees and deltas. Rich farmland often forms along these areas!

mcqs.q: What is the Walker circulation and how does ENSO disrupt it?
options: Clean energy means it doesn't produce any smoke when burned.
Walker circulation is the east-west tropical Pacific atmospheric loop: trade winds push warm water west, air rises in Indonesia, sinks over Peru. El Nino weakens it, La Nina strengthens it.
Walker circulation is the rotation of the Earth around the sun.
El Nino is a current that flows from Peru to Australia.

mcqs.q: Why is 'renewable' not the same as 'clean' energy?
options: Plates move because of ocean tides pulling on the crust.

Renewable means the source replenishes naturally on human timescales; clean means low environmental/health impact. Hydropower is renewable but floods habitats; bioenergy is renewable but can drive deforestation.
All renewable energy sources are clean and have no environmental impact.
Clean energy means it doesn't produce any smoke when burned.
